newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-HODDLE HAILS BRAVE NEW AGE OF STRICTER REFS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HODDLE HAILS BRAVE NEW AGE OF STRICTER REFS.

text.p: New stricter refereeing may be to blame for the odd unfair decision but it has also allowed soccer's most exciting players to shine, England manager Glenn Hoddle said on Monday.
Hoddle, the most gifted England midfielder of his generation in the 1980s, said the recent FIFA clamp-down on tackles from behind and "professional fouls" was beginning to reap dividends.

"One good thing about the new rules is that I think it's taken man-to-man marking out of the game," he told a news conference at the England training camp, where his players were preparing for Wednesday's World Cup qualifier against Poland.
"I don't think we'll see the days of (Italian defender Claudio) Gentile again. You can't get away with the things that they used to get away within the first 10 minutes of matches."
In the 1980s Gentile and a host of equally uncompromising defenders regularly clattered their opponents early in games, secure in the knowledge they would escape punishment.
As a result, players like Diego Maradona, and indeed Hoddle himself, were left bruised and intimidated.
"Football suffered, not just me," Hoddle said. "Look at what they did to Maradona in (the World Cup in) 1982."
"The refs are stricter now and therefore there's more room for a playmaker, although at times I think they've taken things a little too far and some common sense is needed."
While tighter guidelines may have helped liberate England's creative players like Paul Gascoigne and Steve McManaman, the ball-winners in the side need to watch out, Hoddle said.
"You have to think about tackles from behind and you have to think about those places on the pitch where you're going to get booked for it."
He said Paul Ince, always in the thick of things in the centre of the England midfield, had learnt from his time at Inter Milan in Italy.
"I think he's appreciating when to stand in and when to stand off."
And 34-year-old defender Stuart Pearce, nicknamed "Psycho" by his England team mates for his wholehearted approach to his trade, had also mellowed with age, Hoddle said.
"I think there are still times when he needs to calm down a bit though," he added.
